--- name: agent-metrics description: Use when the user wants to install, set up, check or remove agent-meter (token, API-equivalent cost and latency metrics for Claude Code and Antigravity per project, client, task and subagent), asks "how much did this task / project / client cost", "why is my agent slow or expensive", wants a local report or a BigQuery + Looker Studio dashboard, needs to fix unpriced models with "agent-meter pricing", or wants ad-hoc DuckDB / BigQuery queries over the collected metrics. --- # AI Coding Metrics Skill (`agent-metrics`) ## Overview `agent-meter` is an **optional, standalone CLI** that reads the transcripts Claude Code and Antigravity (CLI, IDE and app) already write to disk and turns them into per-project, per-client, per-task and per-subagent metrics: tokens by type, API-equivalent cost (`≈`), cache hit ratio, task latency P50/P95/P99, active time vs wall-clock, parallelism, retries and tool-call counts. - **Option A — Local (default)**: a DuckDB file at `~/.agent-meter/meter.duckdb`, a summary after each task or session, and an offline HTML report. No network, no cloud account. - **Option B — Cloud (opt-in, on top of A)**: a BigQuery replica (dataset `agent_metrics`) loaded with free-tier load jobs, plus a Looker Studio dashboard. The local store stays the source of truth. It only stores numbers and metadata: never prompts, assistant text, code, tool inputs/outputs or file paths. Every cost is **API-equivalent**: it is not what a subscription plan bills. This skill guides the user through installing and configuring the CLI, reading its output and querying the data. It never edits host settings files by hand: `agent-meter setup` does that with consent, a backup and a reversible `agent-meter uninstall`. ## When to Use ### Trigger Scenarios - The user asks to install or configure agent-meter, or to "track how much my agents cost". - The user asks what a task, session, project or client cost, or why a task was slow or expensive. - The user wants a report (local HTML) or a cloud dashboard (BigQuery + Looker Studio). - `agent-meter doctor` or a summary reports unpriced models, a stale scheduler, missing hooks or a cloud backlog. - The user wants an ad-hoc question answered from the metrics (e.g. "cost per subagent type this month"). ### When NOT to Use - **Billing disputes with a provider**: agent-meter shows API-equivalent cost, not invoices. - **Reading prompt or code content**: agent-meter never stores it; do not try to recover it from transcripts. - **Users who did not ask for metrics**: agent-meter is opt-in. Never install it or register hooks unprompted. ## Process ### Phase 1: Install the CLI (Python ≥ 3.11; `uv` provisions it) ```bash uv tool install --python 3.12 "git+https://github.com/jggomez/expert-ai-developer-skills#subdirectory=tools/agent-meter" # or pipx install --python python3.12 "git+https://github.com/jggomez/expert-ai-developer-skills#subdirectory=tools/agent-meter" # Option B also needs the BigQuery extra: uv tool install --force --python 3.12 "agent-meter[bigquery] @ git+https://github.com/jggomez/expert-ai-developer-skills#subdirectory=tools/agent-meter" agent-meter --help ``` If `agent-meter` is not found afterwards, the tool bin directory (usually `~/.local/bin`) is missing from `PATH`: run `uv tool update-shell` and open a new terminal. ### Phase 2: Choose local or cloud and run the wizard Ask the user which option they want before running anything. Explain each wizard prompt as it appears: 1. **Hosts detected**: Claude Code (`~/.claude/`), Antigravity CLI (`~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/`), Antigravity IDE (`~/.gemini/antigravity/`), with how much history exists. 2. **Backfill**: imports existing history once. Re-running is idempotent (nothing is double-counted). 3. **Triggers**: `hooks` (a summary after every task / session), `scheduler` (every 15 min via `launchd` / systemd user timer / cron), both, or none (manual `agent-meter collect`). The wizard shows the exact JSON it will add, backs up the settings file and never overwrites existing hooks. If the optional `agent-metrics` plugin is installed, the wizard skips user-level hooks because the plugin already registers them. 4. **Privacy**: anonymize project names before cloud upload, store subagent descriptions (defaults: no / no). 5. **Projects and clients**: projects are discovered from the imported history; set display names, clients and rates afterwards with `agent-meter projects set`. **Option A — local only** (zero network calls): ```bash agent-meter setup --local # interactive agent-meter setup --local --yes # accept the defaults ``` **Option B — cloud** (always pass the GCP project explicitly; the wizard never relies on the `gcloud` default project): ```bash agent-meter setup --cloud --gcp-project devhack-3f0c2 --mode billing agent-meter setup --cloud --gcp-project my-sandbox-project --mode sandbox ``` - **`billing` mode**: the project has a billing account linked. Load jobs and the free tier keep the cost at $0 for normal volumes. The wizard offers a **$1 budget alert**; tell the user that an alert notifies but **does not cap** spend. - **`sandbox` mode**: BigQuery sandbox, no billing account. Tables expire after 60 days, so the wizard schedules a weekly `agent-meter sync --full-reload` that re-uploads everything from the local store. - Prerequisites the wizard checks, each with the exact fix command: `gcloud` installed, Application Default Credentials valid (`gcloud auth application-default login`), billing linked (billing mode), BigQuery API enabled, and the roles `roles/bigquery.dataEditor` + `roles/bigquery.jobUser` on the project. Offer to run a fix only when the wizard marks it safe. - Running `setup` again is safe: it reports "already configured" instead of duplicating anything. - After the first sync, follow the Looker Studio guide: [Looker Studio dashboard](https://github.com/jggomez/expert-ai-developer-skills/blob/main/docs/agent-metrics/looker-studio.md). ### Phase 3: Verify the installation ```bash agent-meter doctor # config, hooks per host, store, pricing, untracked history, scheduler agent-meter doctor --cloud # adds the GCP prerequisite checks and BigQuery lag/backlog ``` Each line is `OK`, `WARN` or `FAIL` with a fix hint. Exit code `3` means at least one `FAIL`. ### Phase 4: Interpret the metrics ```bash agent-meter last # last session + today and month-to-date for the project, all hosts agent-meter tasks --last 5 # per-task rollups with every subagent agent-meter report --open # offline HTML report (by project, host, day, latency, cache) agent-meter verify --reconcile # store vs a fresh re-read of the transcripts ``` How to read them: - **Cost `≈ $X`** is API-equivalent. **`≥ $X`** means some calls are unpriced: fix them (Phase 5) before trusting totals. - **Cache hit ratio** = `cache_read / (input + cache_read + cache_write)`. A falling ratio means paying more for the same work (context churn, frequent restarts). - **Active time vs wall-clock**: gaps longer than the idle threshold (default 120 s, e.g. waiting for a permission prompt) count toward wall-clock only. **Parallelism** = Σ subagent active time ÷ task active time; > 1 means fan-out saved time. - **Retries** count repeated runs of the same subagent type in one task (e.g. implementer → QA → implementer), i.e. the cost of self-correction loops. - **Cost share by subagent type** shows which role dominates (implementers are usually the largest share). - **Client view**: `agent-meter projects set

--client --billing hourly --rate 40 --currency USD`, then `agent-meter report --client `; correct dev hours with `agent-meter hours set

2026-10 32`. ### Phase 5: Keep prices correct ```bash agent-meter pricing unpriced # models seen without a price agent-meter pricing list agent-meter pricing alias gemini-3.7-flash gemini-3.6-flash --estimated agent-meter pricing add my-model --input 3 --output 15 --cache-read 0.3 --effective-from 2026-10-01 --source-url https://example.com/pricing agent-meter pricing validate ``` Prices are USD per million tokens and versioned by `--effective-from`. Edits re-price history immediately, with no re-ingest. Mark aliases `--estimated` when the price is borrowed from another model. ### Phase 6: Ad-hoc queries **Local (DuckDB)**: open the store read-only. If a collect is running, wait a few seconds and retry. ```bash duckdb -readonly ~/.agent-meter/meter.duckdb \ "SELECT local_month, display_name, round(sum(cost_usd), 2) AS usd, sum(unpriced_calls) AS unpriced FROM v_daily_project_cost GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY local_month DESC, usd DESC LIMIT 20" # without the duckdb CLI: uv run --with duckdb python -c "import duckdb, os; c = duckdb.connect(os.path.expanduser('~/.agent-meter/meter.duckdb'), read_only=True); print(c.sql('SELECT agent_type, round(sum(cost_usd), 2) AS usd FROM v_agent_type_cost GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY usd DESC'))" ``` **Cloud (BigQuery)**: the dataset has views with the same names and columns as DuckDB. Filter on `local_date` / `local_month` to keep scans small. ```bash bq query --project_id=devhack-3f0c2 --use_legacy_sql=false \ 'SELECT local_month, project_id, ROUND(SUM(cost_usd), 2) AS usd FROM agent_metrics.v_daily_project_cost WHERE local_date >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY usd DESC' ``` Useful views: `v_calls`, `v_daily_project_cost`, `v_sessions`, `v_tasks`, `v_agent_runs`, `v_agent_type_cost`, `v_tool_counts`, `v_task_latency`, `v_dev_hours`, `v_client_month`, `v_unpriced_models`, `v_health`. ### Phase 7: Remove it ```bash agent-meter uninstall # removes hooks + scheduler, restores settings; keeps the data agent-meter uninstall --purge --yes # also deletes ~/.agent-meter/ uv tool uninstall agent-meter ``` If the settings file changed after setup, uninstall removes only agent-meter's own entries and keeps the user's later edits. ## Usage ### Example Prompts - *"Set up agent-meter locally for Claude Code and Antigravity."* - *"Connect agent-meter to BigQuery in devhack-3f0c2 with a $1 budget alert."* - *"How much did the last plan execution cost, and which subagent was the most expensive?"* - *"doctor says there are unpriced models; fix the pricing."* - *"Query the cost per client for last month from DuckDB."* ### Commands Reference | Command | Purpose | | :--- | :--- | | `agent-meter setup [--local\|--cloud] [--yes] [--hosts …] [--triggers …] [--gcp-project P] [--mode billing\|sandbox]` | Guided, idempotent setup | | `agent-meter collect [--host H] [--since D] [--full]` | Incremental ingest | | `agent-meter last` · `agent-meter tasks --last N` · `agent-meter report --open` | Summaries and report | | `agent-meter projects …` · `agent-meter hours …` · `agent-meter tag ""` | Projects, clients, dev hours, work items | | `agent-meter pricing list\|unpriced\|add\|set\|alias\|remove\|validate` | Price table | | `agent-meter doctor [--cloud]` · `agent-meter verify --reconcile [--cloud]` | Health and reconciliation | | `agent-meter sync [--full-reload] [--dry-run]` | Upload to BigQuery (Option B) | | `agent-meter config show\|get\|set\|edit` | e.g. `agent-meter config set timezone America/Bogota` | | `agent-meter uninstall [--purge --yes]` | Clean removal | ## Red Flags - Installing agent-meter or registering hooks without the user asking for it (it is opt-in). - Editing `~/.claude/settings.json`, `~/.gemini/config/hooks.json` or `~/.gemini/settings.json` by hand instead of letting `agent-meter setup` / `agent-meter uninstall` do it (the latter file belongs to Gemini CLI and is never touched). - Relying on the `gcloud` default project instead of passing `--gcp-project` explicitly. - Presenting `≈` costs as invoiced amounts, or reporting totals while `unpriced_calls > 0` without saying "≥". - Telling the user a budget alert caps spend (it only notifies). - Opening `meter.duckdb` read-write for ad-hoc queries while the scheduler or a hook may be writing. - Trying to extract prompt text, code or file paths from transcripts to "enrich" the metrics. ## Verification - [ ] The user explicitly chose Option A (local) or Option B (cloud) before `agent-meter setup` ran. - [ ] `agent-meter doctor` (and `agent-meter doctor --cloud` for Option B) shows no `FAIL`. - [ ] `agent-meter last` or `agent-meter tasks --last` prints a summary after the next task. - [ ] `agent-meter pricing unpriced` is empty, or every remaining model is explained to the user. - [ ] Option B: `agent-meter verify --reconcile --cloud` reports 0 differences before building Looker charts. - [ ] Costs were presented as API-equivalent (`≈`), never as billed amounts.

---
name: documentation-expert
description: "Use when writing or cleaning up technical docs: root AGENTS.md, DESIGN.md alignment, Diátaxis guides and Mermaid diagrams, kept short and with checked relative links."
---

# Documentation Expert Skill

## Overview
This skill guides the authoring, structuring, and automated validation of Zero-Fluff technical documentation, root `AGENTS.md` guides, official Google `DESIGN.md` references, and Mermaid.js architectural diagrams. Applying the Diátaxis framework (Tutorials, How-To Guides, Reference, Explanation), it enforces strict line budgets, portable relative links, and zero-boilerplate clarity.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Authoring or auditing READMEs, runbooks, API references, and root `AGENTS.md` (`<= 90 lines`).
- Ensuring documentation aligns with official Google 2-layer `DESIGN.md` (`<= 110 lines`) and `docs/<feature-name>/` line caps.
- Modeling architectures, sequence flows, or schemas with syntax-safe Mermaid.js diagrams.
- Validating markdown heading hierarchy, relative links, and path portability.

### When NOT to Use
- **Authoring MADR architectural decisions (`adr-NNN-*.md`)**: Route to `senior-architect-engineering`.
- **Authoring UI token systems (`DESIGN.md`)**: Route to `ui-ux-designer`.
- **Automated codebase cartography (`project-context.md`)**: Route to `repo-research`.

## Process
### Phase 1: Diátaxis Pillar & Zero-Fluff Budget Alignment
1. Select one Diátaxis mode per section — never mix tutorials, how-to steps, reference tables, and explanations together.
2. Enforce strict **Zero-Fluff** conciseness caps across project and feature artifacts:
   - Root `AGENTS.md <= 90 lines` (verified build/lint/test commands, conventions, links to `DESIGN.md` & `context/memory/MEMORY.md`).
   - Root Google `DESIGN.md <= 110 lines` (YAML tokens + 8 sections) and feature UI delta in `docs/<feature-name>/spec.md` (`## Design <= 30 lines`).
   - Feature specs in `docs/<feature-name>/`: single `spec.md` (`## Product <= 50`, `## Design <= 30`, `## Architecture <= 50`), `adr-NNN-*.md <= 55 lines`, `test-matrix.md <= 80 lines`; verification reports are returned in the reviewer's final message (`<= 50 lines`), never written as files.

### Phase 2: Syntax-Safe Mermaid.js Diagramming
Use concise Mermaid blocks (`flowchart TD`, `flowchart LR`, `sequenceDiagram`, `stateDiagram-v2`, `erDiagram`) instead of prose walls. Always quote labels containing spaces, slashes, brackets, or parentheses (e.g., `api["Auth API (v2)"]`).

### Phase 3: Link Portability & Automated Validation
Use portable repository-relative links (never machine-local paths) and run the validator script:
```bash
python3 ./skills/documentation-expert/scripts/validate_docs.py
```

## Usage
### Commands & Automation Scripts
```bash
# Audit markdown heading hierarchy, relative links, and local path leaks
python3 ./skills/documentation-expert/scripts/validate_docs.py
```

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Run `validate_docs.py` via Bash after authoring or editing markdown docs.
- **Antigravity**: Verify Mermaid quoting, line caps, and relative links via `validate_docs.py`.

## Red Flags
- Bloated prose walls exceeding artifact line budgets (`AGENTS.md > 90`, `DESIGN.md > 110`, reports `> 50` lines).
- Blending How-To recipes with deep theoretical Explanations in the same section.
- Leaking local machine paths or leaving broken relative `.md` links.
- Unquoted parentheses or brackets in Mermaid node labels causing render failures.

## Verification
- [ ] Document matches its target Diátaxis pillar and stays within its Zero-Fluff line cap.
- [ ] Root `AGENTS.md` and `DESIGN.md` cross-links resolve cleanly when present.

name: guidelines-karpathy
description: Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring code to avoid overcomplication, make surgical changes, surface assumptions, and define verifiable success criteria.
---

# Karpathy Guidelines Skill

## Overview
This skill enforces behavioral and architectural restraint to prevent common LLM coding pitfalls, derived from Andrej Karpathy's observations on LLM developer tendencies. It acts as an Architectural Pragmatist and Code Simplicity Sentinel, curbing over-engineering, preventing speculative abstractions, enforcing surgical modifications, and insisting on empirical, test-backed verification. It is deterministically backed by the Anti-Lazy Code Gate (`anti-lazy-code-gate.js`) to block placeholder stubs before session completion.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Pre-implementation sanity checks before generating code or designing solutions.
- Code reviews to evaluate whether a proposed solution is overcomplicated or speculative.
- Debugging and fixing targeted defects where touching adjacent code risks regressions.
- Refactoring tasks to ensure changes remain strictly minimal and goal-driven.

### When NOT to Use
- **Product requirement definition**: Route to `product-analyst`.
- **Automated AST-based code smell detection**: Route to `code-smells-expert`.
- **High-level enterprise architecture frameworks**: Route to `senior-architect-engineering`.
- **CI/CD pipeline and git hook setups**: Route to `build-and-ci-gates`.

## Process
### Rule 1: Think Before Coding
- State technical assumptions explicitly before modifying files. If genuine ambiguity exists, ask the user directly.
- If multiple valid architectural interpretations exist, present them with trade-offs rather than guessing silently.
- If a simpler, lower-code approach exists, propose it. Actively push back against unnecessary complexity.

### Rule 2: Simplicity First (YAGNI)
- Implement the absolute minimum amount of code necessary to solve the problem cleanly.
- Never introduce speculative configurability, unused parameters, or generic abstractions for single-use code.
- Avoid writing defensive error handling for logically impossible internal scenarios.

### Rule 3: Surgical, Minimal Changes
- Touch only the files and lines strictly required to satisfy the goal.
- Match existing repository styling, conventions, and idioms.
- Do NOT "improve", reformat, or refactor adjacent working code or comments unrelated to the task.
- Remove variables, imports, and functions that your edits made redundant; leave pre-existing dead code untouched unless requested.

### Rule 4: Anti-Lazy Code Policy (Deterministic Gate)
- Enforce **zero tolerance** for lazy placeholders or incomplete stubbed code:
  * Prohibited patterns include `TODO: implement later`, `# ... rest of code`, `// ... rest of code`, `pass # placeholder`, `/* unimplemented */`, or bare `raise NotImplementedError`.
- Provide 100% complete, fully implemented, working code in every single edit.
- In both runtime ecosystems, this rule is guarded deterministically by `anti-lazy-code-gate.js`: any diff containing placeholder stubs immediately fails the Stop gate with exit code 2.

### Rule 5: Anti-Premature Abstraction (Premature Abstraction Smell)
- Guard against the **Premature Abstraction Smell**: avoid over-engineering interfaces, generic base classes, factory layers, or strategy patterns when a simple, pure function suffices.
- Follow the Rule of Three: do not extract an abstraction until at least three concrete instances exist and the duplication causes demonstrable maintenance friction.
- Three slightly similar lines of transparent code are far superior to a premature indirection layer that complicates debugging.

### Rule 6: Goal-Driven Execution & Loop Verification
- Establish concrete, verifiable success criteria (e.g. specific tests that must pass) before editing.
- Loop and iterate until tests pass; never assume victory without running the verification command.

## Usage
### Example Prompts
- *"Review this proposed solution against the Karpathy guidelines: are we overcomplicating the architecture?"*
- *"Fix this bug surgically without touching or refactoring any adjacent functions."*
- *"Implement the simplest possible solution for this feature without speculative abstractions or lazy stubs."*

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Keep changes atomic and surgical. The plugin's Stop hook (`anti-lazy-code-gate.js`) automatically guarantees no lazy placeholder stubs are committed.
- **Antigravity**: Apply Karpathy principles during the PLAN and BUILD phases, verified by `anti-lazy-code-gate.js` before task completion.

## Red Flags
- Leaving `TODO: implement later` or placeholder comments instead of writing full implementations.
- Adding "future-proofing" flags, hooks, or interfaces for features not explicitly requested.
- Prematurely creating multi-tiered class hierarchies or factory patterns when a pure function suffices.
- Refactoring or reformatting adjacent working functions during a focused bug fix.
- Declaring a solution complete without executing the relevant test suite.

## Verification
- [ ] Assumptions stated and confirmed before implementing.
- [ ] Minimum lines of code written to solve the problem (zero speculative abstractions).
- [ ] Complete code implementations provided (zero lazy stubs; `anti-lazy-code-gate.js` passes cleanly).
- [ ] Only target files modified; adjacent working code untouched.
- [ ] Automated tests executed and passing cleanly.

## References
For the comprehensive behavioral checklist and review rubrics:
- [Karpathy Behavioral Checklist](references/karpathy-checklist.md)

name: testing-expert
description: "Use when designing automated tests in any language: test cases (TC-XX), hermetic Arrange-Act-Assert suites, Gherkin BDD scenarios and honest reporting of what actually ran."
---

# Testing Expert Skill

## Overview
This skill guides the design, structuring, and validation of hermetic automated tests, Gherkin BDD specifications, and concise IEEE/ISTQB test cases (`TC-XX`). Acting as a Lead QA Architect, it enforces Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) isolation, boundary mocking, concise `docs/<feature-name>/test-matrix.md` (`<= 80 lines`) traceability, and strict **Fail-Honest** execution reporting.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Designing unit, integration, component, and E2E test cases (`TC-XX`) with explicit `Objective`, `Steps`, and `Expected Result`.
- Authoring and validating Gherkin BDD `.feature` files (`Given` / `When` / `Then` / `Examples`).
- Structuring hermetic Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) test suites with isolated boundary mocks.
- Auditing test outcomes to enforce Fail-Honest `BLOCKED` / `SKIPPED` reporting when environments are unavailable.

### When NOT to Use
- **Inner-loop TDD production code authoring**: Route to `test-driven-development` or `code-implementer`.
- **Full State 3 QA execution & matrix sign-off**: Route to `qa-tester`.
- **Live Playwright browser journey & viewport screenshot capture**: Route to `blackbox-tester` (`e2e-blackbox-tester`).

## Process
### Phase 1: Concise IEEE/ISTQB `TC-XX` & Gherkin BDD Design
1. Define each test case (`TC-01`, `TC-02`, ...) concisely for `docs/<feature-name>/test-matrix.md` (`<= 80 lines`):
   - **Objective**: Single behavior, invariant, or boundary under verification.
   - **Steps**: Deterministic precondition + action (`Given`/`When` or concise numbered steps).
   - **Expected Result**: Observable output, state transition, or error contract (`Then`).
   - **Automated Test & Status**: Linked test path/symbol and empirical status (`PASSED`, `FAILED`, `BLOCKED`, `SKIPPED`).
2. When authoring `.feature` specs, use clean `Feature`, `Background`, `Scenario`, and `Scenario Outline` + `Examples` tables.

### Phase 2: Hermetic Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) & Fail-Honest Execution
1. Partition every test into **Arrange** (fixtures + boundary mocks), **Act** (single invocation), and **Assert** (exact behavioral check) with zero shared mutable state across tests.
2. **Fail-Honest Rule**: If a test runner, database service, live web server, or Chromium/Playwright binary cannot run in the current environment, report `BLOCKED` or `SKIPPED` with the exact missing prerequisite — **never** stub assertions, relax thresholds, or fabricate `PASSED`.

### Phase 3: Automated Gherkin Validation
Validate all `.feature` files for missing `Examples:`, step-less scenarios, or ordering errors:
```bash
python3 ./skills/testing-expert/scripts/validate_gherkin.py
```

## Usage
### Commands & Automation Scripts
```bash
# Validate Gherkin .feature syntax across the workspace
python3 ./skills/testing-expert/scripts/validate_gherkin.py
```

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Run `validate_gherkin.py` via Bash and execute targeted test runners with empirical exit-code checks.
- **Antigravity**: Validate `.feature` syntax via `run_command` and record honest `PASSED`/`FAILED`/`BLOCKED`/`SKIPPED` statuses.

## Red Flags
- Claiming `PASSED` when the runner, server, or browser was unavailable instead of reporting `BLOCKED` or `SKIPPED`.
- Bloated test matrices (`> 80 lines`) or vague `TC-XX` entries missing `Objective`, `Steps`, or `Expected Result`.
- Order-dependent tests, live external network calls in unit tests, or `Scenario Outline` blocks missing `Examples:`.

## Verification
- [ ] Every `TC-XX` specifies `Objective`, `Steps`, `Expected Result`, `Automated Test`, and honest `Status`.
- [ ] Gherkin validator exits with code `0`:
  ```bash
  python3 ./skills/testing-expert/scripts/validate_gherkin.py
  ```
- [ ] Unit and integration tests follow strict AAA isolation with external I/O mocked at boundaries.
- [ ] Unavailable runners/browsers are transparently marked `BLOCKED` or `SKIPPED` (zero faked `PASSED`).

## References
- [Software Testing Best Practices Reference](references/testing-best-practices.md)
- [Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) & Gherkin Syntax](references/gherkin-syntax.md)

skills.body:
---
name: commit-expert
description: "Use when writing commit messages or setting up commit checks: Conventional Commits rules, validator scripts and local git commit hooks."
---

# Commit Expert Skill

## Overview
This skill enforces high-quality, readable, and bisectable Git commit histories. It acts as a Git Version Control Specialist and History Architect, ensuring that all commits follow the 7 rules of git messaging, utilize standard Conventional Commits prefixes, maintain atomic boundaries, and validate formatting through automated hook scripts aligned with deterministic branch gates.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Authoring commit messages for staged code changes.
- Setting up or validating local git `commit-msg` hooks.
- Squashing, interactive rebasing, or cleaning up messy commit histories before PR submission.
- Enforcing Conventional Commits standards and branch naming alignment across an engineering team.

### When NOT to Use
- **Authoring Pull Request descriptions or branch reviews**: Route to `pull-request-expert`.
- **Pre-commit quality and linting checks**: Route to `build-and-ci-gates`.
- **Writing application source code**: Route to `code-implementer`.

## Process
### Phase 1: Conventional Commits Specification & Regex Standard
Structure every commit message following the 7 rules of git commit messages and the formal Conventional Commits standard:
1. **Canonical Commit Pattern**:
   ```regex
   ^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)(\([a-z0-9._-]+\))?: .+$
   ```
2. **Permitted Types**:
   - `feat`: A new user-facing feature or API capability.
   - `fix`: A bug fix for existing functionality.
   - `docs`: Documentation-only additions or modifications.
   - `style`: Formatting, missing semicolons, whitespace changes with zero code logic alterations.
   - `refactor`: Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature.
   - `perf`: Code change that improves runtime performance or memory usage.
   - `test`: Adding missing tests or correcting existing tests.
   - `build`: Changes affecting the build system, packaging, or external dependencies.
   - `ci`: Changes to CI configuration files and automation scripts.
   - `chore`: Auxiliary tasks, housekeeping, tool updates.
   - `revert`: Reverting a previous commit.

3. **Branch Gate Alignment (`gitflow-branch-gate.js`)**:
   - Every commit must strictly align with the active branch prefix enforced by `gitflow-branch-gate.js`:
     * Branches prefixed with `feat/*` or `feature/*` must carry commits typed `feat` (or supporting `test`, `docs`).
     * Branches prefixed with `fix/*`, `bugfix/*`, or `hotfix/*` must carry commits typed `fix`.
     * Direct commits to protected branches (`main`, `master`, `develop`, `release/*`) are blocked by `gitflow-branch-gate.js`.

4. **Formatting Constraints**:
   - **Subject Line**: `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>` (50 characters maximum, imperative mood, NO trailing period).
   - **Body (when context is required)**: Separated by a blank line, wrapped at 72 characters, explaining *what* and *why*.

### Phase 2: Atomic Staging & Clean History
1. Stage only logically cohesive changes in a single commit (one feature, fix, or refactor per commit).
2. Use interactive rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~N`) to squash intermediate "wip" or fixup commits before pushing.

### Phase 3: Automated Validation
Validate the commit message format using the automated validator script:
```bash
python3 ./skills/commit-expert/scripts/validate_commit_msg.py .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
```

## Usage
### Commands & Automation Scripts
```bash
# Validate a specific commit message file or git edit message
python3 ./skills/commit-expert/scripts/validate_commit_msg.py .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
```

### Example Prompts
- *"Format a Conventional Commit message for these staged authentication changes."*
- *"Audit the recent 5 commit messages on this branch against the Conventional Commits regex and Gitflow rules."*
- *"Help me set up a local commit-msg git hook to block non-conventional commit messages."*

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Validate commit message files before running `git commit`, ensuring compatibility with `gitflow-branch-gate.js`.
- **Antigravity**: Ensure that every commit created during the COMMIT phase complies with Conventional Commits and branch rules.

## Red Flags
- Commits violating the Conventional Commits regex `^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)...`.
- Vague commit subjects like "fixes", "updates", "wip", or "changes".
- Exceeding 50 characters on the subject line or ending with a trailing period.
- Committing directly to protected branches (`main`, `master`, `develop`) without feature branches.
- Blending multiple unrelated tasks into one giant commit.
- Using past tense (*"added feature"*) instead of imperative mood (*"add feature"*).

## Verification
- [ ] Commit message conforms to `^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)(\([a-z0-9._-]+\))?: .+$`.
- [ ] Commit type aligns with active branch type enforced by `gitflow-branch-gate.js`.
- [ ] Subject is under 50 characters, uses imperative mood, and has no period.
- [ ] Blank line separates subject and body.
- [ ] Automated validation script passes:
  ```bash
  python3 ./skills/commit-expert/scripts/validate_commit_msg.py .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
  ```

## References
- [Git Commit Best Practices & Guidelines](references/commit-guidelines.md)
- [Configuring Git Hooks for Commit Quality](references/git-hooks-setup.md)

# Commit Expert Skill

## Overview
This skill enforces high-quality, readable, and bisectable Git commit histories. It acts as a Git Version Control Specialist and History Architect, ensuring that all commits follow the 7 rules of git messaging, utilize standard Conventional Commits prefixes, maintain atomic boundaries, and validate formatting through automated hook scripts aligned with deterministic branch gates.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Authoring commit messages for staged code changes.
- Setting up or validating local git `commit-msg` hooks.
- Squashing, interactive rebasing, or cleaning up messy commit histories before PR submission.
- Enforcing Conventional Commits standards and branch naming alignment across an engineering team.

### When NOT to Use
- **Authoring Pull Request descriptions or branch reviews**: Route to `pull-request-expert`.
- **Pre-commit quality and linting checks**: Route to `build-and-ci-gates`.
- **Writing application source code**: Route to `code-implementer`.

## Process
### Phase 1: Conventional Commits Specification & Regex Standard
Structure every commit message following the 7 rules of git commit messages and the formal Conventional Commits standard:
1. **Canonical Commit Pattern**:
   ```regex
   ^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)(\([a-z0-9._-]+\))?: .+$
   ```
2. **Permitted Types**:
   - `feat`: A new user-facing feature or API capability.
   - `fix`: A bug fix for existing functionality.
   - `docs`: Documentation-only additions or modifications.
   - `style`: Formatting, missing semicolons, whitespace changes with zero code logic alterations.
   - `refactor`: Code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature.
   - `perf`: Code change that improves runtime performance or memory usage.
   - `test`: Adding missing tests or correcting existing tests.
   - `build`: Changes affecting the build system, packaging, or external dependencies.
   - `ci`: Changes to CI configuration files and automation scripts.
   - `chore`: Auxiliary tasks, housekeeping, tool updates.
   - `revert`: Reverting a previous commit.

3. **Branch Gate Alignment (`gitflow-branch-gate.js`)**:
   - Every commit must strictly align with the active branch prefix enforced by `gitflow-branch-gate.js`:
     * Branches prefixed with `feat/*` or `feature/*` must carry commits typed `feat` (or supporting `test`, `docs`).
     * Branches prefixed with `fix/*`, `bugfix/*`, or `hotfix/*` must carry commits typed `fix`.
     * Direct commits to protected branches (`main`, `master`, `develop`, `release/*`) are blocked by `gitflow-branch-gate.js`.

4. **Formatting Constraints**:
   - **Subject Line**: `<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>` (50 characters maximum, imperative mood, NO trailing period).
   - **Body (when context is required)**: Separated by a blank line, wrapped at 72 characters, explaining *what* and *why*.

### Phase 2: Atomic Staging & Clean History
1. Stage only logically cohesive changes in a single commit (one feature, fix, or refactor per commit).
2. Use interactive rebase (`git rebase -i HEAD~N`) to squash intermediate "wip" or fixup commits before pushing.

### Phase 3: Automated Validation
Validate the commit message format using the automated validator script:
```bash
python3 ./skills/commit-expert/scripts/validate_commit_msg.py .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
```

## Usage
### Commands & Automation Scripts
```bash
# Validate a specific commit message file or git edit message
python3 ./skills/commit-expert/scripts/validate_commit_msg.py .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
```

### Example Prompts
- *"Format a Conventional Commit message for these staged authentication changes."*
- *"Audit the recent 5 commit messages on this branch against the Conventional Commits regex and Gitflow rules."*
- *"Help me set up a local commit-msg git hook to block non-conventional commit messages."*

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Validate commit message files before running `git commit`, ensuring compatibility with `gitflow-branch-gate.js`.
- **Antigravity**: Ensure that every commit created during the COMMIT phase complies with Conventional Commits and branch rules.

## Red Flags
- Commits violating the Conventional Commits regex `^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)...`.
- Vague commit subjects like "fixes", "updates", "wip", or "changes".
- Exceeding 50 characters on the subject line or ending with a trailing period.
- Committing directly to protected branches (`main`, `master`, `develop`) without feature branches.
- Blending multiple unrelated tasks into one giant commit.
- Using past tense (*"added feature"*) instead of imperative mood (*"add feature"*).

## Verification
- [ ] Commit message conforms to `^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)(\([a-z0-9._-]+\))?: .+$`.
- [ ] Commit type aligns with active branch type enforced by `gitflow-branch-gate.js`.
- [ ] Subject is under 50 characters, uses imperative mood, and has no period.
- [ ] Blank line separates subject and body.
- [ ] Automated validation script passes:
  ```bash
  python3 ./skills/commit-expert/scripts/validate_commit_msg.py .git/COMMIT_EDITMSG
  ```

## References
- [Git Commit Best Practices & Guidelines](references/commit-guidelines.md)
- [Configuring Git Hooks for Commit Quality](references/git-hooks-setup.md)

---

# Pull Request Expert Skill

## Overview
This skill guides branch partitioning, commit history auditing, and authoring concise, high-signal Pull Request (PR) descriptions (`<= 40 lines`). Acting as a Lead Release Engineer, it enforces reviewable diffs (`< 200–400 LOC`), Conventional Commits, empirical links to `docs/<feature-name>/test-matrix.md`, and **Fail-Honest** disclosure of any `BLOCKED` or `SKIPPED` verification gates.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Preparing a feature, fix, refactor, or chore branch for Pull Request submission.
- Auditing branch naming and commit messages against Conventional Commits standards.
- Authoring Zero-Fluff PR descriptions (`<= 40 lines`) backed by empirical test evidence.
- Performing pre-PR self-review to catch debug leftovers and verify honest gate statuses.

### When NOT to Use
- **Validating a single local commit message**: Route to `commit-expert`.
- **Authoring CI/CD workflow YAML**: Route to `build-and-ci-gates`.
- **Formal OWASP & architectural sign-off**: Route to `compliance-verifier`.

## Process
### Phase 1: Scope Partitioning & Branch Naming
Keep each PR focused on one cohesive capability (`< 200–400 LOC` when feasible) on a Conventional branch (`feat/<slug>`, `fix/<slug>`, `refactor/<slug>`, `chore/<slug>`).

### Phase 2: Automated Branch & Commit History Audit
Verify branch naming and Conventional Commit compliance across branch commits:
```bash
python3 ./skills/pull-request-expert/scripts/validate_pr_content.py
```

### Phase 3: Self-Review & Concise Fail-Honest PR Description (`<= 40 lines`)
1. Inspect `git diff` to remove stray debug statements (`print`, `console.log`), dead code, or secret leaks.
2. Author a Zero-Fluff PR description strictly `<= 40 lines`:
   - **Summary & Key Changes**: 2–5 bullets stating *why* and *what* changed.
   - **Verification & Test Matrix**: Exact commands executed with exit codes, linking `docs/<feature-name>/test-matrix.md` when present.
   - **Fail-Honest Gate Status**: Explicitly disclose any `BLOCKED` or `SKIPPED` verification gates (e.g., E2E browser checks without a live server/Chromium or unavailable staging env) and why — **never** check off or claim untested checks passed.

## Usage
### Commands & Automation Scripts
```bash
# Validate active branch name and Conventional Commits history
python3 ./skills/pull-request-expert/scripts/validate_pr_content.py
```

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Run `validate_pr_content.py` via Bash, review `git diff`, and draft the `<= 40 lines` PR body.
- **Antigravity**: Run `validate_pr_content.py` via `run_command` and verify honest `PASSED`/`BLOCKED`/`SKIPPED` evidence before drafting the PR.

## Red Flags
- Bloated PR descriptions (`> 40 lines`) or massive multi-topic diffs (`> 500 LOC`).
- Claiming E2E, integration, or manual checks passed when they were `BLOCKED` or `SKIPPED`.
- Omitting `docs/<feature-name>/test-matrix.md` links or empirical test command output.
- Non-standard branch names (`temp`, `fix1`) or leftover debug prints in the diff.

## Verification
- [ ] Branch name and commit history pass validation (`exit code 0`):
  ```bash
  python3 ./skills/pull-request-expert/scripts/validate_pr_content.py
  ```
- [ ] PR description is strictly `<= 40 lines` and links `docs/<feature-name>/test-matrix.md` (when applicable).
- [ ] Every `BLOCKED` or `SKIPPED` gate is transparently disclosed with zero fabricated checkmarks.
- [ ] Full `git diff` is free of debug statements, conflict markers, and secrets.

## References
- [Pull Request & Commit Best Practices](references/pr-best-practices.md)
- [PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md](templates/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md)

skills.body:
---
name: repo-research
description: "Use when opening a codebase you do not know yet: maps its structure, stack, commands and invariants into a codebase map (.agents/rules/project-context.md, at most 80 lines) and bootstraps the root AGENTS.md and context/memory/MEMORY.md."
---

# Repository Research Skill

## Overview
This skill maps a repository's stack, directory boundaries, executable commands, and architectural invariants into a concise, high-signal **Codebase Map** at `.agents/rules/project-context.md` (`<= 80 lines`), while bootstrapping or synchronizing target-project root `AGENTS.md` (`<= 90 lines`) and `context/memory/MEMORY.md` (`<= 80-100 lines`). It prioritizes deterministic script extraction over speculative file reading to conserve tokens.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Onboarding onto an unfamiliar repository or refreshing `.agents/rules/project-context.md`.
- Bootstrapping or syncing a target repository's root `AGENTS.md` and `context/memory/MEMORY.md`.
- Verifying build, lint, and test commands alongside entry points and layer invariants.
- Reconciling contradictions between stale documentation and actual source code.

### When NOT to Use
- **Bulk-reading entire source trees without running `repo_analyzer.py` first**.
- **Deep code smell or SOLID auditing**: Route to `code-smells-expert` or `code-critic`.
- **Feature-level PRD, UI design, or MADR authoring**: Route to discovery skills (`docs/<feature-name>/`).

## Process
### Phase 1: Automated Repository Extraction
Run the analyzer script to extract directory layout, languages, package managers, config files, and entry points into `.agents/rules/project-context.md`:
```bash
python3 ./skills/repo-research/scripts/repo_analyzer.py
```

### Phase 2: High-Signal Codebase Map Refinement (`<= 80 lines`)
Inspect **only** high-signal config and entry files (`pyproject.toml`, `package.json`, `Makefile`, `pubspec.yaml`, main entry points) to replace `[...]` placeholders across the 4 core sections — keeping `.agents/rules/project-context.md` strictly `<= 80 lines`:
1. **Stack & Entry Points**: Verified runtime versions, frameworks, data stores, and entry modules.
2. **Directory & Layer Map**: Concise tree plus domain, interface/UI, and test directory ownership.
3. **Run, Build & Test Commands**: Exact, verified install, dev, lint/typecheck, scoped test, and full test commands.
4. **Key Architectural & Env Invariants**: Layer boundaries, required env vars (names only, zero secrets), and runtime constraints.

### Phase 3: Target `AGENTS.md` & `context/memory/MEMORY.md` Bootstrap/Sync
When researching a target repository:
1. **Bootstrap/Sync Root `AGENTS.md` (`<= 90 lines`)**: If missing or stale, create/update root `AGENTS.md` with verified build/lint/test commands, core coding conventions, and explicit links to root `DESIGN.md` (if UI exists) and `context/memory/MEMORY.md`.
2. **Bootstrap/Sync `context/memory/MEMORY.md` (`<= 80-100 lines`)**: Ensure cross-AI handoff state, active branch, and links to `architecture.md` and `conventions.md` are initialized or synchronized without duplicating full codebase trees.
3. **Surface Contradictions**: Report any mismatch as **Documented** vs. **Actual** vs. **Action Taken**.

## Usage
### Commands & Automation Scripts
```bash
# Generate or refresh .agents/rules/project-context.md from workspace configs
python3 ./skills/repo-research/scripts/repo_analyzer.py
```

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Run `repo_analyzer.py` via Bash, selectively read entry/config files, then refine `project-context.md` (`<= 80 lines`) and sync root `AGENTS.md` + `context/memory/MEMORY.md`.
- **Antigravity**: Execute `repo_analyzer.py` via `run_command` during State 0 orientation, then finalize the Codebase Map and root governance links.

## Red Flags
- Producing bloated 10-section codebase dumps (`> 80 lines`) or speculative prose.
- Reading dozens of source files before running `repo_analyzer.py`.
- Leaving unresolved `[...]` placeholders or unverified run/test commands.
- Failing to bootstrap or synchronize root `AGENTS.md` (`<= 90 lines`) and `context/memory/MEMORY.md` in target projects.

## Verification
- [ ] Analyzer executed cleanly:
  ```bash
  python3 ./skills/repo-research/scripts/repo_analyzer.py
  ```
- [ ] `.agents/rules/project-context.md` is `<= 80 lines` with all 4 sections populated and zero `[...]` placeholders.
- [ ] Target-project root `AGENTS.md` (`<= 90 lines`) and `context/memory/MEMORY.md` (`<= 80-100 lines`) are present and synchronized.
- [ ] All build, lint, and test commands match actual project manifests.

## References
- [Project Context Template](references/project-context-template.md)

skills.body:
---
name: adversarial-challenger
description: "Use when a change touches auth, payments, concurrency, untrusted input or destructive actions and needs to be attacked before release: stress tests, fuzzing, worst-case inputs, failure paths, timeouts and memory pressure."
---

# Adversarial Challenger & Stress Testing Skill

## Overview
This skill implements an adversarial testing philosophy designed to actively attempt to break software components. Operating as an objective, hostile challenger, it subjects systems to worst-case boundary inputs, fuzzing, intentional fault injection, network latency/disconnections, race conditions, and memory/resource saturation. 

Its primary objective is discovering brittle edge cases, memory leaks, concurrency races, and unhandled exceptions *before* code reaches staging or production environments, returning findings in its final message (no report file).

**Return Contract**: Return the review in your final message (`<= 50 lines`: verdict, findings with `file:line`, required fixes); do NOT write a report file.

---

## When to Use

### Trigger Scenarios
- Validating business-critical features (payments, authentication, order processing, state machines) prior to release.
- Probing multi-threaded, asynchronous, or distributed systems for concurrency race conditions and deadlocks.
- Simulating network chaos, slow dependencies, socket timeouts, and intermittent connection drops.
- Fuzzing APIs and interfaces with malformed JSON, boundary integers, null bytes, unicode overflows, and schema violations.
- Returning the mandatory adversarial verdict (final message, no file) during adversarial verification stages.

### When NOT to Use
- **Happy-path functional verification**: Route standard acceptance testing to `qa-tester`.
- **Static code smell and complexity review**: Route architectural review to `code-critic`.
- **Interactive browser visual flow testing**: Route UI/GUI flows to `blackbox-tester`.
- **Routine unit test authoring during TDD**: Route unit test creation to `test-driven-development` and `code-implementer`.

---

## Process

The adversarial probing lifecycle tests resilience across 5 core attack and stress vectors:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Identify Critical Component / API"] --> V1["Vector 1: Boundary & Input Fuzzing"]
    V1 --> V2["Vector 2: Fault Injection & Failure Paths"]
    V2 --> V3["Vector 3: Timeout & Network Chaos"]
    V3 --> V4["Vector 4: Concurrency & Race Conditions"]
    V4 --> V5["Vector 5: Resource & Memory Saturation"]
    V5 --> COMPILE["Aggregate Findings & Severity Ratings"]
    COMPILE --> REPORT["Return report in final message"]
    REPORT --> STATUS{"Any CRIT or HIGH Defects?"}
    STATUS -->|"Yes"| REJECT["VULNERABLE / AT RISK: Escalate to code-implementer"]
    STATUS -->|"No"| APPROVE["RESILIENT: Release verification cleared"]
```

### Phase 1: The 5 Adversarial Vectors

1. **Vector 1: Boundary & Malformed Input Fuzzing**:
   - **Boundary Numerics**: $0$, negative numbers ($-1$, $-2^{31}$), maximum integers ($2^{31}-1$, $2^{63}-1$), float overflows, `NaN`, and `Infinity`.
   - **String Fuzzing**: Empty strings `""`, whitespace-only, 100k-character strings, null bytes (`\x00`), emoji clusters, multi-byte UTF-8 sequences, path traversal strings (`../../etc/passwd`), and SQL/XSS payloads.
   - **Malformed Structures**: Truncated JSON payloads, unexpected field types (arrays instead of strings, objects instead of booleans), missing required keys, extra unexpected keys.

2. **Vector 2: Failure-Path & Fault Injection**:
   - **Downstream Dependency Outages**: Inject mock exceptions simulating third-party HTTP 500, 502, 503, connection refused, or DNS lookup failures.
   - **Filesystem & Database Faults**: Simulate disk-full errors, permission denied, locked records, and transaction rollbacks.
   - **Verification**: Ensure the application fails gracefully, unrolls state changes cleanly, returns consistent error models, and never crashes the process.

3. **Vector 3: Timeout & Network Chaos**:
   - **Artificial Latency**: Simulate downstream responses delayed by 5s, 10s, 30s.
   - **Premature Socket Closes**: Terminate TCP connections mid-payload.
   - **Connection Pool Exhaustion**: Exhaust HTTP client or database connection pools and verify non-blocking queueing or clear timeout errors.

4. **Vector 4: Concurrency, Race Conditions & Deadlocks**:
   - **Parallel Requests**: Send 20-50 simultaneous concurrent requests against the same resource (e.g. concurrent balance deductions or seat reservations).
   - **Idempotency Probes**: Send rapid duplicated requests sharing identical idempotency keys to ensure exactly-once execution.
   - **Locking Invariants**: Verify optimistic or pessimistic locking prevents corrupted intermediate states or negative values.

5. **Vector 5: Resource Saturation & Memory Stress**:
   - **Payload Flooding**: Submit multi-megabyte payloads to observe memory consumption.
   - **Leak Probing**: Execute 1,000 rapid iterations of a workflow while tracking memory growth, unclosed file descriptors, or dangling event listeners.

---

### Phase 2: Severity Classification

- **CRITICAL (`CRIT`)**: Process crash, unhandled panic, data corruption, negative balance/state inconsistency, security/auth bypass under load.
- **HIGH (`HIGH`)**: Unbounded memory growth, thread starvation, infinite socket hang without timeout, uncaught 500 error leaking internal stack traces.
- **MEDIUM (`MED`)**: Inconsistent error response format, slow recovery from downstream failure, missing retry backoff jitter.
- **LOW (`LOW`)**: Sub-optimal error messaging, minor latency jitter under load.

---

### Phase 3: Zero-Fluff Report Returned in Final Message (`<= 50 lines`)

Do NOT write a report file. Return a **Zero-Fluff** report in your final message strictly capped at **`<= 50 lines`** (`<= 20 lines` on clean passes) following the [Adversarial Report Template](references/adversarial-report-template.md). Omit empty per-probe prose sections—output ONLY the compact metadata header, the 5-vector summary table, and actionable defects (or `None.` when `RESILIENT`):

```markdown
# Adversarial Stress & Resiliency Report
```

# Adversarial Challenger & Stress Testing Skill

## Overview
This skill implements an adversarial testing philosophy designed to actively attempt to break software components. Operating as an objective, hostile challenger, it subjects systems to worst-case boundary inputs, fuzzing, intentional fault injection, network latency/disconnections, race conditions, and memory/resource saturation. 

Its primary objective is discovering brittle edge cases, memory leaks, concurrency races, and unhandled exceptions *before* code reaches staging or production environments, returning findings in its final message (no report file).

**Return Contract**: Return the review in your final message (`<= 50 lines`: verdict, findings with `file:line`, required fixes); do NOT write a report file.

---

## When to Use

### Trigger Scenarios
- Validating business-critical features (payments, authentication, order processing, state machines) prior to release.
- Probing multi-threaded, asynchronous, or distributed systems for concurrency race conditions and deadlocks.
- Simulating network chaos, slow dependencies, socket timeouts, and intermittent connection drops.
- Fuzzing APIs and interfaces with malformed JSON, boundary integers, null bytes, unicode overflows, and schema violations.
- Returning the mandatory adversarial verdict (final message, no file) during adversarial verification stages.

### When NOT to Use
- **Happy-path functional verification**: Route standard acceptance testing to `qa-tester`.
- **Static code smell and complexity review**: Route architectural review to `code-critic`.
- **Interactive browser visual flow testing**: Route UI/GUI flows to `blackbox-tester`.
- **Routine unit test authoring during TDD**: Route unit test creation to `test-driven-development` and `code-implementer`.

---

## Process

The adversarial probing lifecycle tests resilience across 5 core attack and stress vectors:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Identify Critical Component / API"] --> V1["Vector 1: Boundary & Input Fuzzing"]
    V1 --> V2["Vector 2: Fault Injection & Failure Paths"]
    V2 --> V3["Vector 3: Timeout & Network Chaos"]
    V3 --> V4["Vector 4: Concurrency & Race Conditions"]
    V4 --> V5["Vector 5: Resource & Memory Saturation"]
    V5 --> COMPILE["Aggregate Findings & Severity Ratings"]
    COMPILE --> REPORT["Return report in final message"]
    REPORT --> STATUS{"Any CRIT or HIGH Defects?"}
    STATUS -->|"Yes"| REJECT["VULNERABLE / AT RISK: Escalate to code-implementer"]
    STATUS -->|"No"| APPROVE["RESILIENT: Release verification cleared"]
```

### Phase 1: The 5 Adversarial Vectors

1. **Vector 1: Boundary & Malformed Input Fuzzing**:
   - **Boundary Numerics**: $0$, negative numbers ($-1$, $-2^{31}$), maximum integers ($2^{31}-1$, $2^{63}-1$), float overflows, `NaN`, and `Infinity`.
   - **String Fuzzing**: Empty strings `""`, whitespace-only, 100k-character strings, null bytes (`\x00`), emoji clusters, multi-byte UTF-8 sequences, path traversal strings (`../../etc/passwd`), and SQL/XSS payloads.
   - **Malformed Structures**: Truncated JSON payloads, unexpected field types (arrays instead of strings, objects instead of booleans), missing required keys, extra unexpected keys.

2. **Vector 2: Failure-Path & Fault Injection**:
   - **Downstream Dependency Outages**: Inject mock exceptions simulating third-party HTTP 500, 502, 503, connection refused, or DNS lookup failures.
   - **Filesystem & Database Faults**: Simulate disk-full errors, permission denied, locked records, and transaction rollbacks.
   - **Verification**: Ensure the application fails gracefully, unrolls state changes cleanly, returns consistent error models, and never crashes the process.

3. **Vector 3: Timeout & Network Chaos**:
   - **Artificial Latency**: Simulate downstream responses delayed by 5s, 10s, 30s.
   - **Premature Socket Closes**: Terminate TCP connections mid-payload.
   - **Connection Pool Exhaustion**: Exhaust HTTP client or database connection pools and verify non-blocking queueing or clear timeout errors.

4. **Vector 4: Concurrency, Race Conditions & Deadlocks**:
   - **Parallel Requests**: Send 20-50 simultaneous concurrent requests against the same resource (e.g. concurrent balance deductions or seat reservations).
   - **Idempotency Probes**: Send rapid duplicated requests sharing identical idempotency keys to ensure exactly-once execution.
   - **Locking Invariants**: Verify optimistic or pessimistic locking prevents corrupted intermediate states or negative values.

5. **Vector 5: Resource Saturation & Memory Stress**:
   - **Payload Flooding**: Submit multi-megabyte payloads to observe memory consumption.
   - **Leak Probing**: Execute 1,000 rapid iterations of a workflow while tracking memory growth, unclosed file descriptors, or dangling event listeners.

---

### Phase 2: Severity Classification

- **CRITICAL (`CRIT`)**: Process crash, unhandled panic, data corruption, negative balance/state inconsistency, security/auth bypass under load.
- **HIGH (`HIGH`)**: Unbounded memory growth, thread starvation, infinite socket hang without timeout, uncaught 500 error leaking internal stack traces.
- **MEDIUM (`MED`)**: Inconsistent error response format, slow recovery from downstream failure, missing retry backoff jitter.
- **LOW (`LOW`)**: Sub-optimal error messaging, minor latency jitter under load.

---

### Phase 3: Zero-Fluff Report Returned in Final Message (`<= 50 lines`)

Do NOT write a report file. Return a **Zero-Fluff** report in your final message strictly capped at **`<= 50 lines`** (`<= 20 lines` on clean passes) following the [Adversarial Report Template](references/adversarial-report-template.md). Omit empty per-probe prose sections—output ONLY the compact metadata header, the 5-vector summary table, and actionable defects (or `None.` when `RESILIENT`):

--- name: blackbox-tester description: "Use when a web UI or user flow changed and needs proof it works in a real browser: runs the user journeys with Playwright, checks console and network errors, and saves screenshots at four screen widths." --- # Black-Box Browser Verification & Visual Testing Skill ## Overview This skill provides deterministic, fail-honest black-box browser verification from the perspective of an actual end user. Operating as a Senior Black-Box QA Engineer, it executes real Chromium browser journeys via **Playwright** (`run_command` / `Bash`), exercises interactive GUI forms, attaches console and network error listeners, captures physical `.png` screenshots across 4 responsive viewports in `docs//evidence/`, and returns a concise Zero-Fluff report (`<= 50 lines`) in its final message. **Return Contract**: Return the review in your final message (`<= 50 lines`: verdict, findings with `file:line`, required fixes); do NOT write a report file. It enforces a strict **Fail-Honest Anti-Hallucination Protocol**: if no web UI exists in scope it immediately returns `SKIPPED`, and if the dev server or Chromium binary cannot run it immediately stops and returns `BLOCKED` with the exact terminal error—never substituting `curl`, `TestClient`, `jsdom`, or static code inspection for a real browser. --- ## When to Use ### Trigger Scenarios - Validating runnable web applications, SPAs, and frontend portals served over HTTP/HTTPS. - Testing real end-to-end user flows (signup, login, navigation, checkout, wizard steps) in a live Chromium DOM. - Auditing GUI form behavior (validation errors, disabled submit states, loading feedback, focus management). - Asserting `0` unhandled JavaScript runtime crashes (`pageerror` / `console.error`) and `0` unexpected HTTP `4xx/5xx` responses. - Capturing physical `.png` evidence across Mobile (`375x812`), Tablet (`768x1024`), Desktop (`1280x800`), and Widescreen (`1920x1080`) viewports in `docs//evidence/`. - Returning the standard verdict in the final message (`<= 50 lines`, no report file) during State 3/4 verification. ### When NOT to Use - **Pure backend/API/CLI/pipeline projects without a web UI**: Immediately return `SKIPPED: No web UI in scope`; route headless API tests to `qa-tester`. - **Unit test creation during coding**: Route to `test-driven-development` or `code-implementer`. - **Static code smell and complexity review**: Route to `code-critic`. - **Adversarial stress and concurrency fuzzing**: Route to `adversarial-challenger`. - **Flutter native mobile apps**: Return `SKIPPED: mobile target, not in scope`. Flutter web is in scope: follow [references/flutter-web-playwright.md](references/flutter-web-playwright.md). --- ## Process The black-box verification lifecycle enforces a mandatory 2-step Pre-Flight before executing real Chromium suites: ```mermaid flowchart TD START["Incoming Verification Request"] --> PF1{"Pre-Flight 1:
Web UI Exists?"} PF1 -->|"No Web UI"| SKIP["Return SKIPPED:
No web UI in scope"] PF1 -->|"Yes"| PF2{"Pre-Flight 2:
URL 200 OK & Chromium Launches?"} PF2 -->|"Server Down / Install Blocked"| BLOCK["STOP & Return BLOCKED:
Exact command & terminal error"] PF2 -->|"200 OK & Chromium Ready"| EXEC["Run Playwright Suite in tests/e2e/
DOM Flows + Console/Net Listeners"] EXEC --> SHOTS["Save 4-Viewport .png Evidence
docs//evidence/"] SHOTS --> REPORT["Return Zero-Fluff Report (<= 50 lines)
in final message"] ``` ### Phase 1: Mandatory 2-Step Pre-Flight & Fail-Honest Gate 1. **Step 1 — Start the App & HTTP `200 OK` Check**: - If no web UI changed, immediately return `SKIPPED: No web UI in scope` without creating fake E2E tests. - Start the app and its backend yourself, using root `AGENTS.md`, then the project's scripts. Never skip because the app is not already running. - Probe the URL to verify it responds with `200 OK`. 2. **Step 2 — Auto-Bootstrap by Stack & Chromium Launch Check**: - If Playwright is not yet installed, auto-bootstrap via `run_command` / `Bash`: * **Python (`pyproject.toml` / `uv`)**: ```bash uv add --dev playwright pytest-playwright && uv run playwright install chromium # Fallback when uv is unavailable: .venv/bin/pip install playwright pytest-playwright && .venv/bin/playwright install chromium ``` * **Node / Frontend (`package.json`)**: ```bash npm install -D @playwright/test && npx playwright install chromium # Respect lockfiles: pnpm add -D @playwright/test && pnpm exec playwright install chromium # yarn add -D @playwright/test && yarn playwright install chromium ``` - Verify `playwright` + `chromium` launches cleanly. - **Strict Fail-Honest Stop**: If the dev server fails to start, the port is unreachable, network policies block Chromium download, or OS shared libraries are missing, **STOP IMMEDIATELY** and return: `BLOCKED: Not executed — ` ### Phase 2: Real Browser Execution (`tests/e2e/`) Write and execute real Playwright E2E tests in `tests/e2e/` running Chromium (headless by default for speed, or `--headed` when live visual observation is requested): - **DOM Journeys & GUI Forms**: Exercise real navigation, form input filling (empty, invalid, boundary, and valid payloads), button clicks, disabled in-flight submit states, and deterministic locator assertions. - **Console & Network Listeners**: Attach `page.on("console")`, `page.on("pageerror")`, and `page.on("response")` listeners asserting **`0` unhandled JS errors** and **`0` unexpected HTTP `4xx/5xx` responses**. ### Phase 2.5: Prove the Data Is Real Use the real backend. A green run against mock data proves nothing. - **No stubs**: Never use `page.route`, `route.fulfill`, `routeFromHAR` or MSW. `check_evidence.py` fails on them. - **Record the run**: Copy `scripts/e2e_recorder.mjs` or `scripts/e2e_recorder.py` to `tests/e2e/`. It writes a `run-*.json` manifest of pages and network requests to the evidence directory. - **`source-on-screen`**: Read a value directly from the source, assert it appears on screen, and record the check. - **`persisted-after-reload`**: After any write, reload and assert the data is still there, then record the check. - **No data source**: Pass `noDataSource: ''` to the recorder. The plan must hold `data-source: none`. - **Approved demo**: Pass `demo: true`. The plan must hold `demo-data: approved`. - **Look at the screens**: Open the screenshots yourself. An empty, broken or error screen is `REJECTED`. ### Phase 3: Mandatory 4-Viewport Screenshot Evidence (`docs//evidence/`) Capture real, non-empty `.png` screenshots saved to `docs//evidence/` across all 4 viewports and assert zero horizontal overflow (`document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= window.innerWidth`): 1. **Mobile (`375x812`)**: Fluid single-column layout, drawer navigation, touch targets $\ge 44 \times 44$ px (`mobile-375x812.png`). 2. **Tablet (`768x1024`)**: Adaptive grid spacing (`tablet-768x1024.png`). 3. **Desktop (`1280x800`)**: Full navigation bar, modals, and hover/focus states (`desktop-1280x800.png`). 4. **Widescreen (`1920x1080`)**: Max-width container alignment (`widescreen-1920x1080.png`). ### Phase 4: Zero-Fluff Report Returned in Final Message (`<= 50 lines`) Verify that Playwright exited `0` **AND** that `python3 scripts/check_evidence.py docs//evidence` (from this skill's directory) exits `0` — it rejects fake or stale PNGs and missing viewports — then return the report in your final message — do NOT write a report file (`<= 50 lines` max, `<= 20 lines` on clean pass) using [references/blackbox-report-template.md](references/blackbox-report-template.md): ```markdown # Black-Box Browser Verification Report - **Feature**: `` | **Date**: `YYYY-MM-DD` | **Target URL**: `http://localhost:3000` - **Runner**: `Playwright Chromium` | **Verdict**: `[PASSED | REJECTED | BLOCKED | SKIPPED]` - **Journeys**: `[X/Y Passed]` | **Unhandled JS Errors**: `0` | **Unexpected HTTP 4xx/5xx**: `0` ## 1. Viewport & Journey Metrics | Viewport | Dimensions | Evidence (`docs//evidence/`) | Overflow-X | Forms & Flows | JS / HTTP Errors | Status | | :--- | :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **Mobile** | `375x812` | `mobile-375x812.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | | **Tablet** | `768x1024` | `tablet-768x1024.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | | **Desktop** | `1280x800` | `desktop-1280x800.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | | **Widescreen** | `1920x1080` | `widescreen-1920x1080.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | ## 2. Actionable Defects None. ``` --- ## Usage ### Invocations & Commands #### Node / Frontend Playwright Suite ```bash # Headless Chromium execution (default) npx playwright test tests/e2e/ # Live visual observation when requested npx playwright test tests/e2e/ --headed ``` #### Python Playwright Suite ```bash # Headless Chromium execution (default) uv run pytest tests/e2e/ --browser chromium # Live visual observation when requested uv run pytest tests/e2e/ --browser chromium --headed ``` ### Example Prompts - *"Execute Playwright black-box browser verification on `http://localhost:3000/checkout` across all 4 viewports and capture `.png` evidence."* - *"Verify sign-up form validation and console/network cleanliness in Chromium and return the verdict with `.png` evidence paths."* ### Host Execution Instructions - **Claude Code**: Bootstrap and run Playwright in `tests/e2e/` via `Bash`; author tests via `Write`/`Edit`; return the report in the final message; verify `.png` evidence via `Glob`. - **Antigravity**: Launch as `e2e-blackbox-tester`; bootstrap and execute Playwright suites via `run_command`; verify physical `.png` files in `docs//evidence/` via `list_dir`; return the concise report in the final message (no report file). --- ## Red Flags - ❌ Reporting `SKIPPED` because the app was not running, instead of starting it. - ❌ Passing a screen tested against stubs, or one nobody compared with its data source. - Using `curl`, `httpx`, `requests`, FastAPI `TestClient`, `jsdom`, or static HTML/JSX code reading as a substitute for a real Chromium browser. - Claiming `PASSED` without Playwright exit code `0` **AND** non-empty `.png` screenshots on disk in `docs//evidence/`. - Fabricating test results instead of returning `SKIPPED` (no web UI) or `BLOCKED` (unreachable server / blocked Chromium binary). - Ignoring `console.error`, `pageerror`, or unexpected HTTP `4xx/5xx` responses. - Using arbitrary `sleep()` calls instead of Playwright auto-waiting locators. - Emitting verbose reports exceeding `50` lines (`<= 20` lines expected on clean passes). --- ## Verification - [ ] Mandatory 2-step Pre-Flight passed (`200 OK` + Chromium launch), or honest `SKIPPED` / `BLOCKED` returned immediately. - [ ] Real Playwright E2E suite in `tests/e2e/` exited with code `0`. - [ ] Console (`console` / `pageerror`) and HTTP response listeners verified `0` unhandled errors. - [ ] Non-empty `.png` screenshots saved in `docs//evidence/` for `375x812`, `768x1024`, `1280x800`, and `1920x1080`, and `scripts/check_evidence.py` exited `0`. - [ ] Concise report (`<= 50 lines`, `<= 20 lines` if clean) returned in the final message; no report file written. --- ## References - Black-Box Report Format (final message): [references/blackbox-report-template.md](references/blackbox-report-template.md)

Never skip because the app is not already running. - Probe the URL to verify it responds with `200 OK`. 2. **Step 2 — Auto-Bootstrap by Stack & Chromium Launch Check**: - If Playwright is not yet installed, auto-bootstrap via `run_command` / `Bash`: * **Python (`pyproject.toml` / `uv`)**: ```bash uv add --dev playwright pytest-playwright && uv run playwright install chromium # Fallback when uv is unavailable: .venv/bin/pip install playwright pytest-playwright && .venv/bin/playwright install chromium ``` * **Node / Frontend (`package.json`)**: ```bash npm install -D @playwright/test && npx playwright install chromium # Respect lockfiles: pnpm add -D @playwright/test && pnpm exec playwright install chromium # yarn add -D @playwright/test && yarn playwright install chromium ``` - Verify `playwright` + `chromium` launches cleanly. - **Strict Fail-Honest Stop**: If the dev server fails to start, the port is unreachable, network policies block Chromium download, or OS shared libraries are missing, **STOP IMMEDIATELY** and return: `BLOCKED: Not executed — ` ### Phase 2: Real Browser Execution (`tests/e2e/`) Write and execute real Playwright E2E tests in `tests/e2e/` running Chromium (headless by default for speed, or `--headed` when live visual observation is requested): - **DOM Journeys & GUI Forms**: Exercise real navigation, form input filling (empty, invalid, boundary, and valid payloads), button clicks, disabled in-flight submit states, and deterministic locator assertions. - **Console & Network Listeners**: Attach `page.on("console")`, `page.on("pageerror")`, and `page.on("response")` listeners asserting **`0` unhandled JS errors** and **`0` unexpected HTTP `4xx/5xx` responses**. ### Phase 2.5: Prove the Data Is Real Use the real backend. A green run against mock data proves nothing. - **No stubs**: Never use `page.route`, `route.fulfill`, `routeFromHAR` or MSW. `check_evidence.py` fails on them. - **Record the run**: Copy `scripts/e2e_recorder.mjs` or `scripts/e2e_recorder.py` to `tests/e2e/`. It writes a `run-*.json` manifest of pages and network requests to the evidence directory. - **`source-on-screen`**: Read a value directly from the source, assert it appears on screen, and record the check. - **`persisted-after-reload`**: After any write, reload and assert the data is still there, then record the check. - **No data source**: Pass `noDataSource: ''` to the recorder. The plan must hold `data-source: none`. - **Approved demo**: Pass `demo: true`. The plan must hold `demo-data: approved`. - **Look at the screens**: Open the screenshots yourself. An empty, broken or error screen is `REJECTED`. ### Phase 3: Mandatory 4-Viewport Screenshot Evidence (`docs//evidence/`) Capture real, non-empty `.png` screenshots saved to `docs//evidence/` across all 4 viewports and assert zero horizontal overflow (`document.documentElement.scrollWidth <= window.innerWidth`): 1. **Mobile (`375x812`)**: Fluid single-column layout, drawer navigation, touch targets $\ge 44 \times 44$ px (`mobile-375x812.png`). 2. **Tablet (`768x1024`)**: Adaptive grid spacing (`tablet-768x1024.png`). 3. **Desktop (`1280x800`)**: Full navigation bar, modals, and hover/focus states (`desktop-1280x800.png`). 4. **Widescreen (`1920x1080`)**: Max-width container alignment (`widescreen-1920x1080.png`). ### Phase 4: Zero-Fluff Report Returned in Final Message (`<= 50 lines`) Verify that Playwright exited `0` **AND** that `python3 scripts/check_evidence.py docs//evidence` (from this skill's directory) exits `0` — it rejects fake or stale PNGs and missing viewports — then return the report in your final message — do NOT write a report file (`<= 50 lines` max, `<= 20 lines` on clean pass) using [references/blackbox-report-template.md](references/blackbox-report-template.md): ```markdown # Black-Box Browser Verification Report - **Feature**: `` | **Date**: `YYYY-MM-DD` | **Target URL**: `http://localhost:3000` - **Runner**: `Playwright Chromium` | **Verdict**: `[PASSED | REJECTED | BLOCKED | SKIPPED]` - **Journeys**: `[X/Y Passed]` | **Unhandled JS Errors**: `0` | **Unexpected HTTP 4xx/5xx**: `0` ## 1. Viewport & Journey Metrics | Viewport | Dimensions | Evidence (`docs//evidence/`) | Overflow-X | Forms & Flows | JS / HTTP Errors | Status | | :--- | :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **Mobile** | `375x812` | `mobile-375x812.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | | **Tablet** | `768x1024` | `tablet-768x1024.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | | **Desktop** | `1280x800` | `desktop-1280x800.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | | **Widescreen** | `1920x1080` | `widescreen-1920x1080.png` | `0px` | `PASS` | `0 / 0` | `PASS` | ## 2. Actionable Defects None. ``` --- ## Usage ### Invocations & Commands #### Node / Frontend Playwright Suite ```bash # Headless Chromium execution (default) npx playwright test tests/e2e/ # Live visual observation when requested npx playwright test tests/e2e/ --headed ``` #### Python Playwright Suite ```bash # Headless Chromium execution (default) uv run pytest tests/e2e/ --browser chromium # Live visual observation when requested uv run pytest tests/e2e/ --browser chromium --headed ``` ### Example Prompts - *"Execute Playwright black-box browser verification on `http://localhost:3000/checkout` across all 4 viewports and capture `.png` evidence."* - *"Verify sign-up form validation and console/network cleanliness in Chromium and return the verdict with `.png` evidence paths."* ### Host Execution Instructions - **Claude Code**: Bootstrap and run Playwright in `tests/e2e/` via `Bash`; ---
name: build-and-ci-gates
description: Implements linters, code formatters, and automated build pipelines (CI/CD) to prevent syntax errors, enforce style consistency, and prevent failing builds from being merged. Use this skill when asked to add linters, configure docker builds, or set up GitHub Actions workflows.
---

# Build and CI Gates Skill

## Overview
This skill establishes automated build pipelines, code quality gates, and Continuous Integration (CI/CD) workflows. It acts as a Build Automation and CI/CD Engineer, ensuring that code styling, linting, typing, and test suites are enforced deterministically by automated systems rather than subjective human debate, blocking defective code before it ever merges.

## When to Use
### Trigger Scenarios
- Running comprehensive local code quality, formatting, and linting checks before committing.
- Configuring or updating CI/CD pipelines (e.g., GitHub Actions workflows).
- Installing local git pre-commit hooks to block defective commits fail-closed.
- Designing containerized multi-stage Docker builds with minimal security attack surface.

### When NOT to Use
- **Authoring unit tests and mocks**: Route to `test-driven-development`.
- **Writing application feature code**: Route to `python-expert` or `code-implementer`.
- **Stand-alone security penetration reviews**: Route to `security-audit`.
- **Diagnosing code design smells**: Route to `code-smells-expert`.

## Process
### Phase 1: Local Code Verification
Before submitting code changes or opening PRs, execute automated formatting and lint checks:
```bash
python3 ./skills/build-and-ci-gates/scripts/run_checks.py
```
If formatting or linting checks fail, immediately fix them using automated tools (e.g., `ruff format`, `black .`, `eslint --fix`).

### Phase 2: Pipeline Integration (CI/CD)
Configure pipeline definitions using pinned versions and deterministic environments:
1. **GitHub Actions**: Scaffold or update `.github/workflows/ci.yml` using the CI template reference.
2. **Containerization**: Use multi-stage `Dockerfile` builds to produce minimal, non-root runner images.
3. **Configuration Pinning**: Pin all linter and formatter settings (`pyproject.toml`, `.eslintrc.json`, `pubspec.yaml`) in repository root.

### Phase 3: Git Hook Automation (Pre-Commit Gate)
Install the automated pre-commit gate to intercept syntax errors, failing tests, or secret leaks locally:
1. Symlink or copy the hook script to `.git/hooks/pre-commit`:
   ```bash
   python3 ./skills/build-and-ci-gates/scripts/pre_commit_quality_gate.py
   ```
2. Ensure the hook fails closed—aborting the commit immediately if any check fails.

## Usage
### Commands & Automation Scripts
```bash
# Run local code verification checks (lint, format, basic tests)
python3 ./skills/build-and-ci-gates/scripts/run_checks.py

# Run pre-commit quality gate check directly
python3 ./skills/build-and-ci-gates/scripts/pre_commit_quality_gate.py
```

### Example Prompts
- *"Set up a GitHub Actions workflow that runs linting, type checks, and tests on every pull request."*
- *"Configure pre-commit hooks to prevent unformatted code or secret leaks from being committed."*
- *"Create a multi-stage Dockerfile for our Python service that runs as a non-root user."*

### Host Execution Instructions
- **Claude Code**: Run `run_checks.py` in the workspace terminal before generating pull requests.
- **Antigravity**: Verify that CI gate checks pass prior to declaring build completion.

## Red Flags
- Committing code without running local linter and formatter gates.
- Configuring pre-commit hooks that fail open (allowing broken commits when tools are missing).
- Building Docker images running as root or leaving compilers and build tools in production images.
- Bypassing CI quality gates with force-pushes or `--no-verify` flags.

## Verification
- [ ] Automated check runner passes cleanly with zero errors:
  ```bash
  python3 ./skills/build-and-ci-gates/scripts/run_checks.py
  ```
- [ ] Pre-commit hook executes and blocks defective commits:
  ```bash
  python3 ./skills/build-and-ci-gates/scripts/pre_commit_quality_gate.py
  ```
- [ ] CI configuration passes schema validation and triggers on pull requests.
- [ ] Production containers build using multi-stage non-root images.

## References
For workflow templates, Dockerfiles, and pre-commit configurations:
- [CI/CD & Lint Templates Reference](references/ci-templates.md)
